message.content:
**Short answer:** The sky looks blue because molecules and tiny particles in Earth’s atmosphere scatter short‑wavelength (blue) light from the Sun more efficiently than they scatter longer‑wavelength (red, orange) light. Our eyes receive a lot of that scattered blue light from every direction, so the sky appears blue. --- ### A little more detail | Step | What happens | Why it matters | |------|--------------|----------------| | 1️⃣ Sunlight reaches Earth | Sunlight is a mixture of all visible colors (red → violet). | The mix would look white if nothing altered it. | | 2️⃣ Light hits the atmosphere | Sun photons encounter air molecules (N₂, O₂) and tiny aerosol particles. | These particles are *much* smaller than the wavelength of visible light. | | 3️⃣ Rayleigh scattering | When light interacts with objects much smaller than its wavelength, the scattering intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴ (inverse fourth power of wavelength). | Short wavelengths (blue ≈ 450 nm) scatter ~10 ×  more than red (≈ 650 nm). | | 4️⃣ Scattered light reaches our eyes | Blue photons are redirected in all directions, filling the sky overhead. | We see that diffuse blue glow all around us. | | 5️⃣ Why not violet? | Violet light scatters even more, but:
• The Sun emits less violet than blue.
• Human eyes are less sensitive to violet.
• Some violet is absorbed by the upper atmosphere. | The net effect makes the sky appear blue rather than violet. | --- ### Why the sky changes color at sunrise and sunset When the Sun is low on the horizon, its light must travel through **many** more kilometres of atmosphere. The longer path gives the short‑blue wavelengths many chances to be scattered out of the direct beam, leaving a higher proportion of reds and oranges to reach our eyes. That’s why the sky near the Sun can turn brilliant reds, pinks, and purples at dawn and dusk. --- ### Quick analogy Imagine a crowded room where a handful of tiny mirrors (the air molecules) are scattered everywhere. If you shine a white flashlight (the Sun) into the room, the mirrors bounce the **blue** part of the light around more than the red part because blue light “jumps” more easily off tiny surfaces. Your eyes see a blue‑tinged glow filling the whole room—that’s the sky. --- **Bottom line:** Blue ≈ short wavelength → scattered a lot → fills the sky → we perceive it as blue.
